figures.title: SchNet: A continuous-filter convolutional neural network for modeling quantum interactions

taxonomy.task: molecular energy and force prediction from atom types and positions

arrangement.units: Three columns separated by thick dashed vertical rules: left = untinted stack of coloured layer boxes (embedding, 3 x interaction, atom-wise, softplus, sum pooling); middle = yellow framed panel 'interaction'; right = salmon framed panel 'cfconv'.
arrangement.inputs_as: serif math tuples (atom types Z, positions r, features x^l) at the top of each column
arrangement.losses_at: no loss drawn; the predicted energy E-hat is a math symbol at the bottom of the left column
arrangement.shared: the positions input is one thick line branching into each interaction layer; the cfconv and interaction internals are drawn once in their own panels

insights.structure: Three columns divided by heavy dashed vertical rules zoom from the full layer stack to the interaction block to the cfconv layer, each expansion a framed panel tinted like the box it expands.
insights.data: Inputs and outputs are only serif math tuples (Z, r, x^l, x^{l+1}, E-hat) at the column tops and bottoms, and each layer box states its type and width ('dense, 64', 'rbf, 300').
insights.emphasis: The novel cfconv layer is the single salmon box in the yellow interaction panel and is expanded into a full salmon panel at the right edge.
insights.flow: Every column reads straight top to bottom along a thick black spine, with the position input entering from the top right as a second thick line that bends left into the layers it conditions.
insights.avoid: The columns carry no (a)/(b)/(c) labels and the 'interaction'/'cfconv' panel names sit small in the bottom-right corners, so a reader who misses the colour match has no textual cue that the columns are zooms.

core.what: three panels separated by dashed vertical rules, each opening a block of the previous one: the full network stack, the yellow 'interaction' block (same yellow as the interaction boxes) and the orange 'cfconv' block (same orange as the cfconv box inside it)

relations.form: left stack's yellow interaction boxes are expanded in the middle yellow panel, whose orange cfconv box is expanded in the right orange panel, tied only by matching fill

every panel reads top to bottom: embedding -> 3 interaction -> atom-wise -> shifted softplus -> atom-wise -> sum pooling -> Ê on the left; atom-wise/cfconv/atom-wise chains in the middle; distance -> rbf -> dense layers on the right
the positions (r1..rn) run down a bus on the right and enter each interaction box and the cfconv box from the side; in the right panel the filter W^l enters a circled * from the side
a thick residual line runs down the left of the interaction panel from x^l to a circled + where v^l joins

channels.colour: fill = block type, carried from overview into the zoom panels (green embedding, yellow interaction, orange cfconv, light blue output layers); white = layers inside an expanded block
channels.shape: rectangles = layers with width written in, circles = combine operations (+, *)
channels.line: thick black lines = per-atom feature and position streams; thin arrows = inputs into blocks
channels.frame: tinted panel = the inside of one block; dashed vertical rules separate zoom levels

quality.strengths: the nested zoom is carried entirely by matching tint, each level getting a full panel; side inputs (positions, the filter W^l) enter at the block that uses them; the main stream is one thick straight line through each panel with the residual join drawn
quality.weaknesses: no molecule or atom-pair geometry is drawn, so the continuous filter is only a stack of named layers; the formula ||ri - rj|| is typeset inside a block; the overview stack gives equal box size to routine output layers and the novel interaction

figures.lesson: Use the fill colour of a layer box in a stack as the background tint of the panel that expands it, so two levels of zoom read without connector lines.

figures.title: Solving Inverse Problems in Medical Imaging with Score-Based Generative Models

taxonomy.task: medical image reconstruction (sparse-view CT / undersampled MRI) via score-based sampling
taxonomy.note: the example data drawn are CT images and sinograms; the paper also covers MRI k-space

arrangement.units: an overview grid (left) and a zoom-in of one step (right), unframed and separated by a vertical dotted rule
arrangement.inputs_as: a small grey 'noise' tag at the top-left of the chain, with measurement y as a circled variable at the bottom right
arrangement.shared: the variables x̂_t, y and ŷ_t appear in both panels

insights.structure: Two panels split by a vertical dotted grey line: left a three-row grid of circled variables (sampled x̂_t, corrected x̂'_t, noisy measurements ŷ_t) from 'noise' to a grey 'results' box with ellipsis columns; right one correction step opened up as data.
insights.data: Variables are white circles with serif math labels; in the right panel the iterate and output are grayscale CT thumbnails and the measurement-domain data are magma-coloured sinogram slabs, three stacked in perspective where masks Λ, I−Λ, λΛ combine.
insights.emphasis: Orange is reserved for everything the method adds (measurement path and correction) against black for unconditional generation, keyed in a grey legend box, and the right panel expands that orange step with real data.
insights.flow: Left panel runs right along the top chain, with orange arrows dropping and rising between rows and long orange curves sweeping from y back to every ŷ_t; right panel runs left to right T → mask combine → ⊕ → T^-1.
insights.avoid: The long orange curves from y back to ŷ_tN and ŷ_tN-1 run under the grid and crowd the legend box; the overlapping perspective slabs make which mask applies to which slab hard to read.

core.what: the reverse diffusion unrolled as a node lattice: a top row x̂_tN -> x̂_tN-1 -> ... -> x̂_t0 -> results in black, with an orange row of measurement-corrected nodes x̂' below it and an orange row of noised measurements ŷ_t fed from y underneath

relations.form: left panel: columns of circled variables per time step (x̂, x̂', ŷ) with ellipsis columns standing for the omitted steps, read left to right
at each step an orange arrow from ŷ_ti below and from x̂_ti above meet at x̂'_ti, which feeds diagonally into the next column's x̂
the same lattice carries both procedures: black arrows along the top row = unconditional generation, orange arrows = inverse-problem solving, keyed in a grey legend box
right of a dotted vertical rule, one step x̂_ti -> x̂'_ti is redrawn on data

the right panel draws the step on images: a CT slice is transformed by T into a colour-mapped sinogram, mixed with the measured sinogram via (1-λ)Λ, I-Λ and λΛ on labelled arrows, summed and mapped back by T^-1

channels.colour: arrow colour = procedure (black unconditional, orange inverse-problem solving), keyed; the sinograms keep their own magma colour map
channels.shape: circles = variables at a time step, rounded grey box = results, real images = the data in the zoom panel
channels.line: solid arrows only; the dotted vertical rule separates overview from detail
channels.frame: a grey tinted box marks the legend and the 'noise' tag

quality.strengths: the measurement-conditioning row is drawn as a second lattice under the unconditional chain so what is added reads as geometry; the zoomed step is drawn on real CT/sinogram images with the mixing weights as arrow labels rather than boxed formulas
quality.weaknesses: the orange arcs from y to ŷ_tN and ŷ_tN-1 sweep under the whole panel as the longest lines; the zoom panel is not tied to a specific step on the left; 'results' is an empty grey box

figures.lesson: Separate the generative chain from the measurement correction purely by arrow colour (black vs orange, legend below), then open one correction step beside it as images that move into the measurement domain, get masked with y, and come back.

figures.title: Score-based diffusion models for accelerated MRI

taxonomy.task: accelerated MRI reconstruction

arrangement.units: a chain of unenclosed image thumbnails above, and one green rounded box with four flat bars as the zoomed-in step
arrangement.inputs_as: real MR images: pure-noise x_T at top left and the aliased measurement y at bottom left
arrangement.shared: y feeds every reverse step by dotted lines

insights.structure: A top row of seven square MR thumbnails (x_T noise through x_{t+2}...x_{t-1} to x_0) forms the reverse-SDE chain, and below it at the bottom right one step (x_{t+1} to x_t) opens into a green rounded box holding four tall bars: Predictor, Data consistency, Corrector, Data consistency.
insights.data: Every state is a real knee MR image whose noise fades left to right, and the aliased measurement y is a real image at bottom left whose dotted navy lines rise into each step arrow and run into the expanded box.
insights.emphasis: A single long cyan 'Reverse SDE' arrow over the chain names the process, and the zoom-out box with a green outline and colour-coded bars (mint predictor, cyan corrector, the two DC bars sharing grey-blue) carries the method's contribution.
insights.flow: Left to right on thick navy block arrows across the top; a green dashed line drops from the x_{t+1} arrow into the step box, which runs left to right with thin black arrows and exits as x_t on a dashed arrow.
insights.avoid: The dotted y lines join only two of the step arrows and then trail off into '...', so it is unclear that y conditions every step; draw the conditioning into all steps or say so.

core.what: the reverse SDE as a row of real MR images from pure noise x_T to the clean x_0, joined by thick navy arrows under one long light-blue 'Reverse SDE' arrow

relations.form: seven image tiles left to right (x_T, x_t+2, x_t+1, x_t, x_t-1, x_0) with ellipses for skipped steps, noise decreasing visibly
the aliased measurement image y sits under x_T and sends dotted navy lines up into the arrows between steps
a green dotted line drops from the x_t+1 arrow into a green rounded box below the row that expands one step
inside the green box four tall bars left to right: Predictor -> Data consistency -> Corrector -> Data consistency, with y entering the box and x_t leaving on a dashed arrow

channels.colour: navy = sampling arrows and measurement lines; green = the zoomed step (callout line, box outline, Predictor bar); light blue = Corrector; grey-blue = both data-consistency bars
channels.shape: image tiles = states, tall rounded bars = sub-steps
channels.line: thick solid arrows = diffusion steps, dotted = measurement injection and the zoom callout, dashed = the step's output
channels.frame: one green rounded frame = the inside of a single step

quality.strengths: every state is a real image, so the noise-to-image progression and the aliased measurement are visible as data; y enters each step from below on its own lines rather than a single wire; the zoom box makes the predictor-corrector-with-data-consistency structure explicit
quality.weaknesses: the zoomed step's output x_t is a dashed arrow to empty space, not tied back to the x_t tile; dotted lines carry both measurement injection and the zoom callout; the detail box shows no data between sub-steps and y's entry into each data-consistency bar is not drawn

figures.lesson: The sampling chain is a row of real image thumbnails going from noise to the clean scan under one long process arrow, with the measured aliased image below sending dashed conditioning lines up into the steps.

figures.title: Concurrent Spatial and Channel 'Squeeze & Excitation' in Fully Convolutional Networks

taxonomy.task: attention module for segmentation CNNs

arrangement.units: four unframed panels each with a centred caption below; a grey-filled notation box at bottom left
arrangement.inputs_as: a white 3-D wireframe feature cuboid U (C x H x W)
arrangement.shared: the same U cuboid and the same squeeze glyphs recur across panels (b)-(d)

insights.structure: Four captioned panels in a 2 x 2 grid: (a) a small top-left schematic of the encoder-decoder before and after inserting red SE blocks, (b) cSE and (c) sSE as single-path blocks, and (d) the largest, bottom-right, stacking sSE above cSE and summing them.
insights.data: The input U is a white wireframe cuboid labelled C, H, W, and each output is a cuboid whose faces are tinted to show the reweighting: vertical coloured slices for channel excitation, a 2 x 2 quadrant of blue/yellow/red/green for spatial excitation, both on the scSE output.
insights.emphasis: The colour of the output cuboids makes the difference between channel and spatial recalibration visible at a glance, and the combined block in (d) is the largest panel.
insights.flow: Left to right in each panel: U branches into a squeeze path (thin bars or a 2 x 2 map with sigma) and a skip that meets it at a circled x, then a circled + in (d) merges the two recalibrated cuboids.
insights.avoid: The panel captions mislabel the blocks ('Spatial Squeeze and Channel Excitation (cSE)' and the scSE caption repeats 'Channel Excitation'), and the grey notation legend is wedged into the bottom-left corner; check captions against the method and give the legend its own row.

core.what: panel (d) stacks the spatial-excitation branch (top) and the channel-excitation branch (bottom) from one input cube U, each redrawn exactly as in panels (c) and (b), and joins their recalibrated cubes at a circled + into Û_scSE

relations.form: (b) cSE and (c) sSE as separate panels, each from a white cube U to a recalibrated cube, captioned with their names
in (d) the two branches split from U, each multiplies U at a circled x, and curved arrows bring both outputs to a circled + 'Add'

feature maps are 3-D cubes with C, H, W edges; channel recalibration colours the cube in vertical slices along C, spatial recalibration colours it in quadrants over H x W, and the combined cube shows both
within each branch: global pooling glyph or 1x1 conv -> thin vectors z (C, C/2, C) or map q -> σ -> x with U
(a) a before/after pair of small U-shaped F-CNN schematics joined by a green arrow 'Insert SE blocks after every encoder & decoder block', the inserted blocks drawn as red bars

channels.colour: in the cubes, colour = excitation weights (slice colours for channel, quadrant colours for spatial); in (a), blue = encoder/decoder, peach = bottleneck, red = SE block; peach also fills the Û_cSE cube's front face, so peach carries two unrelated meanings
channels.shape: cubes = feature tensors, thin bars = channel vectors, small grids = spatial maps, circled x/+ = recalibration and addition
channels.line: solid arrows; operator symbols (⋆ conv, σ) are labels on the arrows, keyed in a legend box
channels.frame: only the legend box is framed; panels separated by whitespace and captions

quality.strengths: the tensors are drawn and recalibration is shown by how the output cube is coloured (slices vs quadrants vs both), so what each block changes is visible; (d) reuses the (b) and (c) drawings so the combination reads by recognition
quality.weaknesses: the four panels sit on an irregular grid ((b) top right, (c) mid left, (d) bottom right) with the legend in the remaining corner; panel (a) uses a separate colour code; operator notation like ⋆^{C/2}_{1x1} is typeset on small arrows

figures.lesson: Show what an attention block reweights by colouring its output cuboid - per-channel slices in different tints for channel attention, a 2 x 2 coloured quadrant pattern for spatial attention, both on the combined block - against a plain white input cuboid.

figures.title: Segment Everything Everywhere All at Once

taxonomy.task: universal interactive segmentation with multimodal prompts

arrangement.units: (a) the architecture with two dotted zoom boxes at its right edge, (b) the interaction loop, side by side and captioned below
arrangement.inputs_as: the words 'Class/Sentence', a real photo and small drawn visual prompts (blob, scribble, box, point) beside a photo along the bottom edge
arrangement.losses_at: no loss drawn; class and mask embeddings as two grey token rows at the top of (a)
arrangement.shared: the SEEM decoder appears in both panels, redrawn as a gradient bar in (b) with the same prompt-token colours

insights.structure: Panel (a) stacks encoders, a joint representation bar, token rows and the decoder from bottom to top, with two dotted zoom boxes stacked at its right; panel (b) repeats the decoder small inside a loop diagram.
insights.data: Every input type becomes a labelled row of coloured squares (green queries, purple image features, orange text, pink memory, blue visual prompt), and visual prompts are drawn literally as tiny thumbnails of a blob, scribble, box and point.
insights.emphasis: The method name SEEM is bold italic with an eyes icon on the decoder bar, and the prompt-type colours recur in the attention zoom and the interaction panel to tie the contribution together.
insights.flow: Short up-arrows carry inputs from the bottom encoders to the top embeddings in (a); dashed lines lead right to the zoom boxes; in (b) dashed red curves loop from the decoder out to the robot and person icons and back into the memory and visual prompt rows.
insights.avoid: Many small elements in thin type (zoom boxes, emoji, faint striped decoder fill) make the figure hard to read at column width, and the two zoom boxes are crowded against panel (a).

core.what: five coloured token rows (learnable queries, image features, text prompt, memory prompt, visual prompt) placed side by side under one wide SEEM Decoder band, fed from encoders whose fills match their tokens

relations.form: Text Encoder (orange), Image Encoder (purple) and Visual Sampler (blue) at the bottom feed a 'Joint Image-Text Representation Space' bar, above which the token rows sit in one line under the decoder
a dotted callout box at the upper right draws cross-attention and self-attention as arcs over a row of coloured tokens, showing which token types attend to which
two dashed lines open the decoder into the attention callout and the Visual Sampler into a second callout: image-feature tokens and a scribble mask -> Mask Pool -> Interpolate -> blue visual tokens
visual prompt types are drawn as a row of small glyph squares under the Visual Sampler: an outline, a scribble, a box, a point and an image

(b) a SEEM-Decoder with memory/text/visual prompt tokens, and red dashed curved arrows forming a 'Machine Loop' (robot icon) back into the memory prompt and a 'Human Loop' (person icon) back into the visual prompt

channels.colour: fill = token/prompt type (green queries, purple image, orange text, pink memory, blue visual), held across the encoders, the token rows, the callouts and panel (b); the decoder band shows all these colours as faded stripes; grey = output class/mask embeddings
channels.shape: small squares = tokens, rectangles = modules, small framed glyphs = visual prompts, emoji icons = machine and human actors
channels.line: solid arrows = data flow; dashed lines are used both for zoom callouts in (a) and for the interaction loops in (b)
channels.frame: dotted boxes = zoomed detail; no frame around (a) or (b)

quality.strengths: token type is a single colour code used everywhere, so the prompts the decoder fuses are visible as data; attention is drawn as arcs over a token row rather than a box; the visual prompt sampler is opened to show how a scribble becomes tokens
quality.weaknesses: the class and mask embedding outputs at the top have no arrow from the decoder; the joint representation space is an empty bar; dashed lines mean both 'detail of' and 'interaction loop'; the loops in (b) are long thin curves out to icons

figures.lesson: Give every input type its own token colour and tint the encoder that produces it in the same colour, so a later attention zoom can show which token types interact without a legend.

figures.title: Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models

taxonomy.task: LLM reasoning by sampling several chain-of-thought paths and voting on the answer
taxonomy.note: family other: LLM prompting / decoding-time reasoning; architecture other: no network drawn, only a language-model box queried by a prompt

arrangement.units: two unframed rows separated by a grey dashed horizontal rule, each named by a bold label at the left; the lower row about three times the height of the upper
arrangement.inputs_as: a one-word 'Prompt' box in the top row; the full quoted few-shot prompt (Q/A exemplars and the test question) in a tall rounded box in the bottom row
arrangement.losses_at: none drawn (training-free); the vote is drawn as converging lines into the final answer box at the right
arrangement.shared: the language model is drawn once per row as an identical grey box; the shared prompt is linked across rows by a hollow downward block arrow

insights.structure: Prior method above a dashed rule as one short Prompt -> Language model -> output -> answer row; the proposed method below with the same order but three parallel output rows between the model and one final answer.
insights.data: Inputs and outputs are quoted verbatim: the full few-shot prompt in a tall white box and each reasoning path as its own text, with the answer split off into a bold cell at the right of each path.
insights.emphasis: New steps are named in blue bold labels with blue dashed marks, and the aggregated answer is the only darker-green fill; path colours mark answers that agree (green) or not (red).
insights.flow: Thin grey curves fan out from the language model to the three paths and converge from their answer cells onto the final answer; a hollow block arrow drops from the top prompt to the bottom prompt to say the same prompt is reused.
insights.avoid: The marginalisation step is a blue dashed annotation arrow that leaves the dashed box, loops up past the label and comes down onto the answer, a detour that duplicates the converging grey lines.

core.what: greedy chain-of-thought as one red path in a short row above a dashed rule, against self-consistency below, where three sampled paths fan out from the same model box and converge on one green answer

relations.form: the two methods stacked in rows with the same left-to-right order (prompt, language model, reasoning, answer), separated by a grey dashed rule, ours below and larger
three sampled reasoning paths stacked as equal-width two-cell boxes (reasoning | answer), their answer cells aligned in one column
thin curved lines from the three answer cells converge on a single darker-green 'The answer is $18.' box at the right
prompt -> language model -> outputs -> answer along one horizontal axis in each row

channels.colour: output fill = whether the path's answer agrees with the majority (pale green $18) or not (pale red $14, $26), darker green = the aggregated answer; blue = annotation of the new steps (labels and dashed marks); grey = the language model
channels.shape: rounded rectangles throughout: white = prompt input, grey = model, tinted = generated text; a split box = one sampled path with its answer cell
channels.line: thin grey curves = data flow; blue dashed = annotation (grouping box and the 'marginalize' arrow); grey dashed rule = separator between methods; hollow block arrow = the same prompt reused
channels.frame: a blue dashed rectangle = the set of sampled reasoning paths

quality.strengths: the fan-out from one model box into three paths and their convergence on one darker answer makes sample-then-vote readable before any label; data is drawn as real quoted prompt and reasoning text; answers are split into their own aligned column so the vote's inputs line up; the proposed row gets most of the area while the prior method is a compact single row
quality.weaknesses: the two rows do not align: the top prompt is a one-word box while the bottom quotes the prompt in full, so the two language-model boxes sit at different x positions and the shared steps cannot be compared column by column; the 'marginalize' step is a looping blue dashed annotation wire rather than an aggregation node; the quoted few-shot prompt fills the left third of the lower row, more space than the step it represents

figures.lesson: Show sample-then-vote as geometry: one model box fans out into several quoted outputs whose answers sit in one aligned column, and their lines converge on a single darker answer box.

figures.title: Self-Instruct: Aligning Language Models with Self-Generated Instructions

taxonomy.task: self-generated instruction data

arrangement.units: unenclosed icons with bold 'Step N' headings; generated examples as stacked rounded cards with a 'Task' tab
arrangement.inputs_as: a checklist icon captioned '175 seed tasks'
arrangement.shared: the Task Pool database is both start and end of the loop; the same LM robot icon recurs at three steps

insights.structure: A clockwise loop with no boxes: seed tasks and the Task Pool at top left, Step 1 and Step 2 across the top, two Step 3 branches (Yes / output-first and No / input-first) returning leftward in the lower middle, and Step 4 Filtering at bottom left pointing back to the pool.
insights.data: Steps are flat clip-art icons (checklist, database cylinder, monitor with question bubble, funnel with gears), and generated data are white stacked cards with a dark-blue 'Task' tab holding real example instructions, inputs, labels and outputs.
insights.emphasis: Real example text in the cards does the explaining, and small robot 'LM' icons mark exactly which steps call the language model.
insights.flow: Thick lavender-to-purple gradient arrows run left to right along the top, turn down the right edge, split at a junction into Yes/No arrows pointing left into the two card stacks, then curve left into Filtering and diagonally back up to the Task Pool.
insights.avoid: The decorative gradient arrows and clip-art icons carry no information and the Step 4 return arrow is a vague diagonal; keep the loop but use plainer arrows and a clear return path.

core.what: a clockwise bootstrapping cycle: seed tasks and the Task Pool database at top left, generation steps across the top, instance generation returning leftward along the bottom, and Step 4 Filtering pointing back up into the pool

relations.form: the Task Pool cylinder is both the start and the end of a closed loop of thick gradient arrows running top-left -> top-right -> down the right edge -> back left -> up into the pool
four bold 'Step N' headings placed above their icon or card along the loop give the order without boxes
after Step 2 the right-edge arrow splits into a Yes / Output-first branch and a No / Input-first branch, each ending in its own stacked 'Task' card one above the other under one Step 3 heading
the Task Pool is drawn as a database cylinder in the loop's top-left corner, the store every generation step reads from and filtering writes back to

channels.colour: carries no data meaning: every arrow has the same blue-to-violet gradient and the clip-art icons are multicoloured decoration; the dark-blue 'Task' tab marks a generated task card
channels.shape: clip-art icons = steps or the store (checklist, database, monitor with question bubble, funnel); white tabbed card stacks = generated data with real example text; a small robot icon = a language-model call
channels.line: one style only: thick soft gradient arrows for the data flow; branch conditions (Yes/No) and strategy names (Output-first/Input-first) are labels on the arrows
channels.frame: none around steps; the card outline frames one generated task

quality.strengths: The loop is real geometry closing on the pool, so the bootstrapping idea reads without labels; generated data is drawn as cards with real instructions, inputs, labels and outputs; the robot 'LM' icon placed on each arrow where the model is called shows exactly which steps use the LM; the Yes/No branch is a clean split into two stacked outputs.
quality.weaknesses: The arrows from the two Step 3 cards into Filtering are two broken curved stubs that bend round the left edge, and the filter-to-pool return is a detached diagonal stub, so the loop's lower-left corner reads as fragments; the Step 2 icon (monitor with a question bubble) does not say 'is it a classification task'; the gradient on arrows is decoration with no meaning.

figures.lesson: Draw each generated artifact as a tabbed card stack holding one real example (instruction, input, output) and mark every model call with the same small robot icon on its arrow, so the pipeline reads as concrete data moving around a cycle.

figures.title: Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection

taxonomy.task: retrieval-augmented generation with self-critique

arrangement.units: two unboxed side-by-side panels separated by rules, each with 'Step N' text sections; a bottom strip repeats both
arrangement.inputs_as: a real prompt in a grey chip at the top of each panel
arrangement.shared: the same prompt, retriever icon and LM network glyph appear in both panels

insights.structure: A narrower baseline RAG panel at left and a wider 'Ours' Self-RAG panel at right, split by a solid grey vertical rule, with a dotted horizontal rule cutting off a bottom strip that repeats both on a second prompt where Self-RAG skips retrieval.
insights.data: Everything is one worked example in real text: grey prompt chips, retrieved passages in grey rounded boxes numbered by black circled digits, generations in green, errors in red underline, and reflection tokens (Retrieve, Relevant, Irrelevant, Supported, Partially, No Retrieval) as small coloured chips.
insights.emphasis: The Self-RAG title is in red, its panel is wider, and the coloured reflection chips plus the ranking '1 > 3 > 2' in Step 3 show the critique that the baseline lacks.
insights.flow: Top to bottom by blue-numbered 'Step N:' headings; inside steps, dashed grey curved arrows fan from the retriever magnifier to three parallel 'Prompt + k' columns, and a blue dashed arrow loops the chosen segment back to the LM for the next round.
insights.avoid: The panels are dense with small type, callout bubbles overlap the baseline's output text, and a stray red '4' badge sits in the final output; keep fewer words per step and keep callouts clear of the text.

core.what: baseline RAG in a narrower left panel and Self-RAG ('Ours') in a wider right panel, split by a vertical rule, both run on the same prompt, with a bottom strip repeating the comparison on a prompt that needs no retrieval

relations.form: two side-by-side panels on the same prompt separated by a solid vertical rule, ours on the right and wider; a dotted horizontal rule cuts off a second, one-line comparison below
within each panel numbered 'Step N:' headings run top to bottom (retrieve, generate, critique)
a magnifying-glass retriever beside the flow returns passages drawn as data: grey rounded boxes with real text, numbered by black circled digits that are reused as tokens later
Self-RAG Step 2 draws three parallel columns 'Prompt + 1/2/3', each with its own LM glyph, generated segment and reflection-token chips
Step 3 ranks the three segments in one row with large '>' signs (1 > 3 > 2), the winner circled in blue and fed back to the LM by a blue dashed arrow

channels.colour: green text = supported generation and red underlined text = contradicted or irrelevant content; reflection-token chips are filled green (Relevant/Supported), red (Irrelevant), orange (Partially) or outlined brown (Retrieve); red is also used for the 'Ours: Self-RAG' title, so red carries both 'wrong' and 'ours'; blue marks 'Step N' labels
channels.shape: grey rounded chips = prompts and passages; small rectangular coloured chips = reflection tokens; a network glyph = the LM; a magnifier = the retriever; black circled digits = passage ids
channels.line: grey dashed curves = passages routed from the retriever to prompts; solid grey short arrows = generation; a blue dashed arrow = the selected segment fed back
channels.frame: panels are delimited by rules, not boxes; a blue rounded outline marks the selected segment in Step 3

quality.strengths: Both methods run on the same real prompt with real passages and generations, so the difference is shown as data, not described; reflection tokens appear as coloured chips exactly where they are emitted; the 1 > 3 > 2 ranking makes the critique step visible as an ordering; the bottom strip shows the no-retrieval case in one line per method.
quality.weaknesses: The two panels are not drawn with the same layout, so the steps do not align across the rule for a direct comparison; red means both 'erroneous' and 'ours' (title); long grey dashed curves from the retriever through the 1-2-3 digits to the three prompts cross the right panel; Step 3 is dense with small chips and text.

figures.lesson: Running the baseline and the method on the same worked example in adjacent panels, with errors set as red underlined text and the method's judgements as coloured chips beside each segment, lets a reader compare the outcomes without reading every sentence.

figures.title: Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback

taxonomy.task: iterative self-refinement of LLM output

arrangement.units: four flat pastel boxes with drop shadows, no containers; whole figure inside a thin black frame
arrangement.inputs_as: a small pale-blue 'Input' box
arrangement.shared: one central Model M box used by both loops

insights.structure: A symmetric figure-eight: a lavender Model M box in the centre with a pale-blue Input box above, a pink Feedback box on the left and a peach Refine box on the right, each tied to the model by an outgoing arc from its top and a returning arc into its bottom.
insights.data: There is no data drawn; the model box holds a line-art brain-circuit icon with a light bulb, and each step's meaning is a one-line caption on a light-grey strip beneath its side.
insights.emphasis: Very thick black curved arrows and oversized serif labels in the side boxes make the two-loop idea the whole figure; circled numerals 0, 1, 2 on the arrows give the order.
insights.flow: Input drops down into the model (0), arcs out left and back from Feedback (1), then out right and back from Refine (2), reading left to right across the bottom captions.
insights.avoid: With no example input or output the figure could describe any iterative method; pair the loop with a concrete text example as the paper's second figure does.

core.what: a symmetric figure-eight: one central Model M box with a Feedback loop arcing out to the left and a Refine loop arcing out to the right, both returning into the same model

relations.form: two closed loops of thick black curved arrows, each leaving the model from its top side and returning into its bottom side, around one centre box
a single Model M box sits at the centre and both loops pass through it, showing that one model plays every role
circled numerals 0 (Input into the model from above), 1 (feedback arc) and 2 (refine arc) on the arrows give the order

channels.colour: one pastel fill per role: pale blue = input, lavender = the model, pink = feedback, peach = refine; it identifies each box and carries nothing else
channels.shape: all steps are flat rectangles with drop shadows; the model box holds a brain-circuit icon
channels.line: one style: very thick black curved arrows for control flow
channels.frame: a thin black frame around the whole figure; grey strips beneath the side boxes hold one-line captions

quality.strengths: The method is the loop, and the figure is nothing but the loop: one model in the centre with two symmetric cycles makes 'the same model gives feedback and refines' visible at a glance; the numbered arrows fix the order without extra text.
quality.weaknesses: No nouns are drawn: no output, feedback text or refined output appears, so what passes round the loop must be read from the grey captions; 'Feedback' and 'Refine' are drawn as boxes beside the model although they are the model's own calls, so the boxes look like separate modules; the arcs are long sweeping curves rather than short paths; the stopping condition is not shown.

figures.lesson: For a self-feedback method, put one model box at the centre and draw each role (critique, revise) as its own loop of thick curved arrows out of and back into that same box, numbering the arrows to fix the order.

figures.title: Self-supervised Graph Learning for Recommendation

taxonomy.task: self-supervised graph collaborative filtering

arrangement.units: two horizontal lanes split by a double rule; each stage is a small square-framed thumbnail with a bold label below
arrangement.inputs_as: a bipartite user-item graph thumbnail in a square frame
arrangement.shared: the GCN model icon is repeated in all three paths (shared encoder)

insights.structure: Two rows separated by a double horizontal rule: the main supervised path on top (graph, GCN model, representation, L_main) and the self-supervised path below, where the graph splits into two parallel sub-rows, each with an augmentation panel of three variants ED, ND, RW divided by dashed vertical lines.
insights.data: The user-item graph is a small bipartite thumbnail (yellow user circles left, blue item circles right) whose augmented copies show dropped edges as dashed lines and dropped nodes as dashed circles; representations are vertical stacks of small coloured cell columns.
insights.emphasis: Repeating the same GCN icon and representation grid in both rows makes the added SSL branch read as a copy with augmentation, and the representation grids differ in colour between the two views.
insights.flow: Left to right in each row along thin black lines; the two lower sub-rows merge by right-angle lines into one circle for L_ssl.
insights.avoid: The top row has a long empty arrow from Graph Structure to the GCN icon and the GCN icons are tiny and illegible; drop the dead space and use a legible model glyph.

core.what: two horizontal lanes split by a double rule: the supervised path (graph -> GCN -> representation -> L_main) on top and the self-supervised path below, whose graph forks into two augmented sub-rows that rejoin at L_ssl

relations.form: a main lane and an SSL lane stacked one above the other, separated by a double horizontal rule, with their GCN and representation columns aligned vertically
the same GCN icon is drawn three times in one column (main lane and both SSL sub-rows), signalling one shared encoder
each augmentation is drawn on a copy of the small bipartite user-item graph: dropped edges as dashed lines, dropped nodes as dashed circles
inside each augmentation panel the three operators ED, ND and RW sit side by side, separated by dashed vertical dividers, with subscripts 1 and 2 for the two views
the two SSL sub-rows' representation grids are joined by lines converging on one L_ssl circle at the right
each lane reads left to right: graph, (augmentation), GCN, representation, loss

channels.colour: in the graphs yellow = user nodes and blue = item nodes; the representation grids use yellow, blue, green and grey columns with no key, so colour there is unexplained
channels.shape: square-framed thumbnails = stages (graph, GCN, representation); open circles = losses; circles in the graph = nodes
channels.line: dashed = a dropped edge or node inside the graph thumbnails, and also the dividers between ED/ND/RW, so dashing carries two meanings; solid arrows = data flow between stages
channels.frame: a square frame per stage thumbnail; one rectangle encloses the three augmentation variants of each view

quality.strengths: The augmentations are shown on the actual data structure (dashed dropped edges and nodes on a toy bipartite graph), so ED/ND/RW are understood without text; aligned columns make the main and SSL lanes directly comparable and the repeated GCN reads as shared; the two views converge on L_ssl as a pairing.
quality.weaknesses: The main lane's arrow from Graph Structure to the GCN runs across a wide empty span, so the routine path takes as much width as the new SSL branch; the GCN icon is too small to read; representation grids are coloured without meaning; dashes mean both 'dropped' and 'divider'; losses are empty circles with no indication of what is compared.

figures.lesson: Stack the main task as a thin top row and the added self-supervised branch below it, both starting from the same small bipartite graph thumbnail, and draw each augmented view as a copy of that graph with the dropped edges and nodes dashed.

figures.title: Show-o: One Single Transformer to Unify Multimodal Understanding and Generation

taxonomy.task: one transformer for multimodal understanding (captioning, VQA) and generation (text-to-image, inpainting, mixed-modality) over discrete text and image tokens

arrangement.units: three task columns marked by headers and dashed rules, crossed by full-width bars (tokenizer, transformer, de-tokenizer) that are each one rounded rectangle
arrangement.inputs_as: real images (a child's rainbow drawing, a man on a bench, a mountain lake, hands slicing an avocado), a white inpainting mask, and quoted prompts or questions next to them
arrangement.shared: tokenizer, transformer and de-tokenizer are each one bar spanning all three task columns

insights.structure: Tasks are columns and the shared components are full-width bars crossing them, so every task visibly passes through the same tokenizer, transformer and de-tokenizer.
insights.data: Inputs and outputs are real images and quoted text; each task's sequence is a row of keyed token cells (text blue, image yellow, masked grey, task tokens orange/purple) above and below the transformer.
insights.emphasis: The transformer band is the tallest and only saturated element, with a gradient fill and the model's coloured wordmark.
insights.flow: Top to bottom: inputs, tokenizer bar, input token rows, thin grey curved lines with arrowheads through the transformer to output token rows, de-tokenizer bar, outputs.
insights.avoid: The gradient fill and multicoloured wordmark of the transformer encode nothing, and the curved lines through it are faint and bend diagonally, so which input cells feed which output cells is hard to follow.

core.what: one Show-o transformer band spanning three task columns, each column's token rows entering above and leaving below it

relations.form: tokenizer, transformer and de-tokenizer are each one rounded bar spanning all three task columns
three task columns side by side under dashed-rule headers: understanding, visual generation, mixed-modality generation
top to bottom in every column: inputs, tokenizer, input token row, transformer, output token row, de-tokenizer, outputs
each task's prompt drawn as a token row with a task token first, image tokens yellow, text tokens blue and masked tokens grey, so the input format is visible per task

channels.colour: token fill = token kind (orange/purple special task tokens, yellow image, blue text, grey masked), keyed in the bottom legend; the transformer's green-to-orange gradient and coloured wordmark are decorative and unkeyed; light blue fills both tokenizer bars and the text-token cells
channels.shape: wide rounded bars = shared components, small squares = tokens, photos and quoted text = data
channels.line: thin grey curved arrows = token positions through the transformer; dashed rules = column headers and legend boundaries
channels.frame: no frames around columns; rounded bars mark components

quality.strengths: The shared single model is geometry (one band across all task columns); every task's input and output sequences are drawn as keyed token rows directly above and below it; real images and quoted prompts show each task; space goes to the transformer.
quality.weaknesses: The transformer's gradient and multicoloured wordmark carry no meaning; the curved lines inside it are faint and diagonal; light blue is used for both tokenizer bars and text tokens; columns are only marked by headers, so outputs in the bottom row are loosely aligned with their inputs; 'Causal & Full Attention' is written but not drawn.

figures.lesson: To say 'one model for all tasks', put the tasks in columns and draw the model as one band spanning every column, with each task's input and output token rows aligned above and below it.

figures.title: Sigmoid Loss for Language Image Pre-Training

taxonomy.task: memory-efficient sigmoid image-text loss across devices
taxonomy.note: training 'other' = pairwise sigmoid (binary) loss over all image-text pairs, the paper's replacement for the softmax contrastive loss

arrangement.units: four matrix panels left to right, separated by whitespace only, one per step of the loss computation
arrangement.inputs_as: column headers I1..I12 (images) and row headers T1..T12 (texts) grouped by device
arrangement.losses_at: a 'loss' bar under each matrix (from the second on), split into one segment per device; the last one sums across devices
arrangement.shared: devices are drawn as coloured header strips repeated in every panel; the row-device order rotates between panels to show the swap

insights.structure: Four copies of the same 12 x 12 text-by-image matrix stand in a row, one per computation step, each with device-coloured header strips on its top and left edges.
insights.data: Pairs are cells: '+' on the diagonal for positives, '-' for negatives, a check mark for cells already counted, and the cells being computed now filled yellow inside a device-coloured outline.
insights.emphasis: Only the current block is bright yellow with a thick coloured border while everything finished fades to pale cells, so each panel shows exactly what one device holds at that moment.
insights.flow: Panels read left to right; small coloured arrows drop from each matrix's columns into a per-device loss bar whose percentages (33%, 66%, check) track progress, ending in a 'Cross Device sum' arrow.
insights.avoid: Nothing in the panels names the steps (no step titles or numbers), so the reader needs the caption to know that the rotating row-device labels mean a cross-device swap.

core.what: four copies of the same 12 x 12 text-by-image pair matrix in a row, one per step of the chunked sigmoid-loss computation, the block computed at each step highlighted in yellow inside a device-coloured outline

relations.form: four identical matrix panels left to right separated only by whitespace; finished cells fade to ticks and a loss bar under each panel fills from 33% to 66% to complete
each panel is a pair matrix with text rows T1..T12 and image columns I1..I12: '+' on the diagonal for positive pairs, '-' elsewhere for negatives
three devices are drawn as coloured header strips on the top and left edges of every matrix; the row-device order rotates between panels to show the text chunks being swapped
small coloured arrows drop from each column into a per-device loss bar, and the last panel's three device segments converge by arrows on 'Cross Device Sigma'

channels.colour: pink, purple and blue = Device 1, 2, 3 consistently on headers, block outlines, minus signs and loss segments; yellow fill = the block being computed now; pale green ticks = pairs already counted; one meaning each
channels.shape: cell glyphs encode the pair state: '+' positive, '-' negative, check mark already done
channels.line: thick coloured outlines = the block one device holds now; short coloured arrows = per-column contribution to the loss
channels.frame: each device block is one outlined square; each panel is one step

quality.strengths: The method (which pairs each device computes at each step, and how text chunks rotate between devices) is drawn as geometry on the pair matrix itself; device colour means one thing everywhere; the progressively filling loss bar shows accumulation without text; the four panels are identical copies so only the change is seen.
quality.weaknesses: The panels carry no step numbers or titles, so the first (all-grey, no loss bar) panel's role as the starting state must be inferred; the rotation of row-device labels between panels is the key move but is shown only by small header changes; cell glyphs and percentages are very small.

figures.lesson: To explain a distributed computation, repeat the same matrix once per step and colour rows, columns and loss bars by the device that owns them, so the reader tracks ownership by colour alone.

figures.title: A Simple Framework for Contrastive Learning of Visual Representations

taxonomy.task: contrastive self-supervised image representation learning

arrangement.units: One unframed diagram: two mirror columns of symbols above a shared input circle.
arrangement.inputs_as: an outlined circle with the symbol x (no image), and two outlined view circles reached by arrows labelled with sampled augmentations t ~ T, t' ~ T
arrangement.losses_at: top, as a horizontal double arrow labelled 'Maximize agreement' between z_i and z_j
arrangement.shared: the shared encoder f(.) and head g(.) appear only as identical arrow labels in both columns

insights.structure: One input circle at the bottom centre forks into two mirror columns of symbols (view circle -> h -> z), joined horizontally at two levels by labelled double arrows.
insights.data: Data and features are math only: outlined circles for x and its two views, bare bold symbols for h and z, with no image or tensor drawn.
insights.emphasis: The two horizontal double arrows carry the message as words: 'Maximize agreement' across the top between z's and 'Representation' between the h's, marking what is trained and what is kept.
insights.flow: Bottom-to-top: diagonal arrows labelled with the sampled augmentations climb from x to the views, then straight vertical arrows labelled f(.) and g(.) rise in each column.
insights.avoid: With no boxes or tint, f and g read as edge labels rather than networks, so a reader cannot see that the two columns share weights; a richer method would need explicit modules.

core.what: one input x at the bottom forks into two mirror columns (view -> h -> z) that face each other, with a horizontal double arrow 'Maximize agreement' between z_i and z_j at the top

relations.form: the two columns are mirror images and the objective is a horizontal double arrow spanning the gap between their top symbols z_i and z_j
the encoder f(.) and head g(.) appear only as identical arrow labels in both columns, implying shared weights without drawing them
each column reads bottom to top: augmented view circle, f(.) arrow, h, g(.) arrow, z
two diagonal arrows labelled t ~ T and t' ~ T leave the input circle to the two view circles, showing two independent augmentations

channels.colour: none: the figure is monochrome black on white
channels.shape: outlined circles = data (x and its two views); bare bold symbols = representations h and z; modules exist only as arrow labels
channels.line: single-headed arrows = transformations, labelled with the function or the sampled augmentation; double-headed horizontal arrows are used both for the objective ('Maximize agreement') and for an annotation ('Representation', marking which level is kept), so one line style carries two meanings
channels.frame: none

quality.strengths: The compared representations z_i and z_j are drawn and face each other across the objective, so what is compared is visible as geometry; h is drawn and marked as the kept representation, separating the trained-on level from the used level; all paths are short and straight.
quality.weaknesses: No image or augmented sample is drawn, so 'views' are abstract circles; the shared encoder is never drawn as one module, only implied by repeated labels; the same double-arrow style means both 'loss' and 'this is the representation'.

figures.lesson: A whole framework can be drawn as a math diagram: circles for data, bare symbols for intermediates, functions as arrow labels, and the objective as a labelled double arrow across the top — enough when the method has few parts.

figures.title: SimMIM: a Simple Framework for Masked Image Modeling

taxonomy.task: masked image modelling pre-training by raw-pixel regression
taxonomy.note: paradigm: SimMIM is concurrent with MAE (both regress raw pixels of masked patches); listed under MAE as the closest founding masked-image-modelling method in the list

arrangement.units: One unframed diagram: input grid at the lower left, a patch row along the bottom right, two stacked model boxes above it, and prediction/target patch rows at the top right.
arrangement.inputs_as: a real photo divided into a 3x3 grid of patches, then a row of patch thumbnails with masked ones drawn as hatched squares
arrangement.losses_at: top, as red vertical double arrows between each predicted patch and its original, with the 'l1 loss' label to the left of the row
arrangement.shared: none

insights.structure: An L-shaped layout: a patch grid at lower left feeds a horizontal masked patch row, above which an encoder box and a one-layer head box are stacked, topped by predicted and target patch rows.
insights.data: Patches are real photo crops, masked ones are grey hatched squares, and predictions are the same crops rendered blurred and faded so prediction vs target reads by image quality.
insights.emphasis: One dark-red accent colours every model outline, arrow and loss double arrow, and only the masked columns have outputs above them, so the loss visibly applies to masked positions only.
insights.flow: Right along the bottom ('Mask' arrow), then up through encoder and head, and finally vertical red double arrows between the two top patch rows.
insights.avoid: The large empty region above the input grid at the upper left leaves the figure lopsided; the input could sit higher or the figure be tighter.

core.what: a row of predicted patches faces a row of target patches directly above it, joined column by column by red l1 double arrows that exist only over the masked positions

relations.form: predicted (faded) patches and target (sharp) patches stacked in two rows with a vertical red double arrow per masked column, labelled 'l1 loss' once at the left
the masking is drawn on the image itself: a real photo cut into a 3 x 3 patch grid at lower left, then the patch row with masked patches replaced by grey hatched squares

an L-shape: the patch grid at lower left feeds right via a 'Mask' arrow into the patch row, which rises bottom to top through the Encoder box and the One-layer Prediction Head box to the prediction row

channels.colour: one dark-red accent is used for every module outline, flow arrow and loss arrow, so it marks 'the method' without distinguishing module from objective; patch colours are the photo's own
channels.shape: photo crops = visible patches and targets; grey hatched squares = masked patches; wide rectangles = model blocks
channels.line: single-headed red arrows = data flow; double-headed red arrows = the l1 comparison
channels.frame: each module is one outlined rectangle spanning the patch row's width

quality.strengths: The defining choice (predict raw pixels, loss only on masked patches) is visible as geometry: only the masked columns have a prediction and a double arrow above them; data are real image crops and masked patches are drawn as hatched data, not described; the module boxes are compact while the patches dominate.
quality.weaknesses: No arrow leads from the prediction head to the predicted row, so where the faded patches come from is implied; the same dark red marks modules, flow and loss; the 'Mask' arrow enters the patch row from its lower-left corner rather than continuing a straight line; the faded predictions are illustrative blurs, not model outputs.

figures.lesson: For masked prediction, stack the predicted patches directly under their target patches, column-aligned with the masked slots below, and join each pair with a short coloured double arrow labelled with the loss.

figures.title: Exploring Simple Siamese Representation Learning

taxonomy.task: self-supervised image representation learning
taxonomy.note: training tag: SimSiam has no EMA teacher; it predicts the stop-gradient output of its own other branch, the closest listed value is self-distillation

arrangement.units: Two unframed vertical branch columns separated by whitespace, joined at the bottom by a rounded split line and at the top by the 'similarity' label.
arrangement.inputs_as: text label 'image x' only, no picture; views named x1, x2 as italic labels beside the column feet
arrangement.losses_at: top centre, as the bare word 'similarity' where both branch lines meet; no box
arrangement.shared: the shared encoder is drawn twice, once per branch, as identical light-blue boxes with the same label 'encoder f'

insights.structure: Two mirror columns rise from one input: the left holds encoder f plus a predictor h box, the right holds encoder f alone, and both lines converge at the top on a single 'similarity' word.
insights.data: Data are never drawn: the image and its two views are only italic labels (image x, x1, x2) at the column feet.
insights.emphasis: The predictor is the only orange box against two light-blue encoders, and stop-grad is a separate dashed arrow with an 'x' beside the right branch, so the two design choices are the only visual differences.
insights.flow: Reading runs bottom-to-top: the rounded split at the bottom forks into the columns, each goes straight up, and the tops bend inward with arrowheads pointing at 'similarity'.
insights.avoid: The stop-grad mark floats beside the right column instead of sitting on its output line, so which edge it cuts is inferred rather than shown.

core.what: two mirror columns rise from one 'image x' and their output lines meet at a single 'similarity' word at the top, the left column carrying an extra predictor and the right a stop-grad mark

relations.form: the two columns' outputs turn inward at right angles and meet at the word 'similarity' centred between them
two identical light-blue 'encoder f' boxes at the same height, one per column, signal one shared encoder
the asymmetry between the branches is drawn by difference alone: an orange 'predictor h' box only on the left, a dashed 'stop-grad' arrow with an x only on the right
each column reads bottom to top from the bracket under 'image x' through x1/x2 and the encoder to the top

channels.colour: light blue = the shared encoder; orange = the predictor, the one added module; one meaning each
channels.shape: rounded rectangles = modules; data (image x, views x1, x2) are only italic labels, never drawn
channels.line: solid grey = forward pass; a grey dashed downward arrow crossed by an x = blocked gradient (stop-grad)
channels.frame: none

quality.strengths: With only five elements the two design choices (predictor on one side, stop-grad on the other) are the only visual differences between otherwise identical columns, so the contribution is seen by contrast; colour carries one meaning per hue; lines are short and orthogonal.
quality.weaknesses: The compared representations (p1 and z2) are not drawn: both lines end at a bare word 'similarity', so what is compared must be read from text; no image or augmented view is drawn; the stop-grad arrow floats beside the right branch instead of sitting on the path it blocks.

figures.lesson: Show a Siamese method's asymmetry by keeping both branches identical except for one differently tinted extra box on one side and a crossed dashed arrow labelled 'stop-grad' beside the other side's output.

figures.title: SlowFast Networks for Video Recognition

taxonomy.task: video action recognition

arrangement.units: two unframed horizontal lanes (Slow on top, Fast below) separated by whitespace, each a row of input frame stack plus three cuboid stages; a single tall prediction bar spans both lanes at the right
arrangement.inputs_as: stacks of flat grey slanted parallelograms standing for frames (4 sparse vs ~15 dense), captioned 'Low frame rate' / 'High frame rate'
arrangement.losses_at: none drawn; only the 'prediction' bar at the right end
arrangement.shared: the prediction head is one tall bar spanning both lanes, its gradient blending the two lane tints

insights.structure: Two unframed horizontal lanes, Slow on top and Fast below, each run frames -> three cuboid stages, and both converge into one tall prediction bar at the right edge.
insights.data: Frames are grey slanted parallelograms whose count (4 vs ~15) encodes frame rate, and feature tensors are 3-D cuboids whose width and depth encode C,T vs βC,αT, labelled in italics on their edges.
insights.emphasis: The contribution is the contrast itself: blue wide cuboids vs green thin cuboids, with the prediction bar's blue-to-green gradient showing the two pathways merging.
insights.flow: Both lanes read left to right with straight black arrows, and after each stage a vertical arrow rises from the Fast lane into the Slow lane's horizontal arrow as a lateral connection.
insights.avoid: The axis glyph floats between the lanes with no frame, and the blocks have only faint radial tints so the blue/green coding nearly disappears in print.

core.what: two horizontal lanes, a Slow pathway on top fed by four frames and a Fast pathway below fed by many frames, run side by side through three feature stages and converge into one tall prediction bar at the right

relations.form: two unframed lanes stacked top and bottom, each frames -> three cuboid stages, aligned so stage k of each lane sits in the same column
vertical arrows rise from the Fast lane into the Slow lane's horizontal arrow after each stage (lateral connections), and both lanes end in one shared prediction bar

the rate and capacity contrast is drawn as geometry: 4 vs about 15 grey frame parallelograms, and wide shallow blue cuboids (C, T) vs thin deep green ones (beta C, alpha T), with a small H,W / T / C axis key between the lanes
each lane reads left to right from frames to feature cuboids to prediction

channels.colour: blue = Slow-pathway features, green = Fast-pathway features; the prediction bar's blue-to-green gradient shows the two merged; frames are neutral grey
channels.shape: slanted parallelograms = input frames; 3-D cuboids = feature tensors whose proportions encode channel and temporal size; a tall bar = prediction
channels.line: one style: solid black arrows for both the lane flow and the lateral connections
channels.frame: none; lanes are separated by whitespace

quality.strengths: The method's whole claim (low frame rate with many channels vs high frame rate with few channels) is drawn as geometry: frame count and cuboid proportions show it before any label is read; colour means pathway and nothing else; the representations are drawn as tensors between input and prediction; all arrows are short and straight.
quality.weaknesses: The lateral connections are plain arrows into the Slow lane's line, so how the two are fused (the transform and concatenation or sum) is not shown; the axis key sits floating between the lanes; the prediction bar does not show the pooling and concatenation it stands for.

figures.lesson: Show a two-rate design by drawing the same stages twice with shape-encoded dimensions (wide shallow cuboids vs thin deep ones, labelled C,T vs βC,αT) and joining them with vertical lateral arrows, so the ratio is visible without a table.

figures.title: SmoothQuant: Accurate and Efficient Post-Training Quantization for Large Language Models

taxonomy.task: post-training activation smoothing for quantization
taxonomy.note: architecture: a per-channel scaling transform migrating difficulty between activations and weights, not a network

arrangement.units: two unboxed halves divided by a dashed rule, each a written matrix product
arrangement.inputs_as: tiny integer matrices X and W with real numbers
arrangement.shared: the same matrix layout and colour scale on both sides

insights.structure: Two halves split by a dashed vertical rule, 'Original:' at left and 'SmoothQuant:' at right, each writing out the product X * W with the actual matrices.
insights.data: Matrices are grids of integer cells on a grey-beige base, heat-tinted by magnitude (outlier -16 in purple-red, 8 and -9 orange), with per-channel abs-max vectors in dashed boxes beside each matrix (a row under X, a column right of W).
insights.emphasis: The heat tint makes the activation outlier jump out on the left and visibly flatten on the right, where the transform equations for X-hat, W-hat and s sit above and below.
insights.flow: Left half to right half; within a half, X then a star then W, with small 'Abs Max' arrows marking the reduction axis.

core.what: the same product X * W written out twice with real numbers, 'Original' at left and 'SmoothQuant' at right of a dashed vertical rule, so the activation outlier visibly shrinks on the right

relations.form: two halves split by a dashed vertical rule, each a 2 x 4 activation matrix times a 4 x 3 weight matrix with the same layout, before on the left and after on the right
the smoothing is shown on toy matrices of integer cells: the left X holds a -16 outlier, the right X-hat has it reduced to -4 while the matching row of W-hat grows to 4 -4 -4
per-channel abs-max vectors sit beside their matrices in dashed boxes (a row under X, a column right of W), with 'Abs Max' arrows along the axis they reduce over

channels.colour: a heat tint on cells = magnitude (purple-red for the largest, orange, then yellow, grey-beige for small values), one meaning throughout
channels.shape: solid-bordered grids = matrices; dashed-bordered strips = the per-channel abs-max vectors
channels.line: arrows labelled 'Abs Max' give the reduction direction; the dashed vertical rule separates before from after
channels.frame: each matrix is one bordered block; the halves are titled 'Original:' and 'SmoothQuant:'

quality.strengths: The method's effect is shown as data: the same matrices with real values before and after, and the heat tint makes the outlier stand out on the left and flatten on the right with no reading; the abs-max vectors are drawn as their own dashed strips next to the matrix they summarise.
quality.weaknesses: The transform itself is carried by typeset equations (X-hat, W-hat, s) under and above the right half rather than by drawn elements; the scale vector s is never drawn moving from X to W, so the migration of difficulty is inferred from changed numbers; the right half shows no abs-max column for W-hat, so the before/after layouts are not fully parallel.

figures.lesson: Put each matrix's per-channel abs-max as a dashed-outline vector right beside it, tinted with the same heat colours as the cells, so the outlier channel and the way the transform spreads it between activation and weight are visible before and after.

figures.title: Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding

arrangement.units: nine unframed text lines, one per decoding iteration
arrangement.inputs_as: quoted text: each line starts with a [START] token and the real sentence so far
arrangement.shared: the accepted prefix is repeated in black on every following line

insights.structure: Nine left-aligned lines stacked top to bottom, each one decoding iteration, with the new tokens always at the right end.
insights.data: Data is a real sentence in bold monospace, every token underlined by a tick-ended bracket that shows its boundaries.
insights.emphasis: Green accepted, red struck-through rejected and blue corrected tokens at each line's end carry the whole idea against the black accepted prefix.
insights.flow: Read each line to its coloured tail, then drop to the next line, which repeats the prefix in black and extends it.
insights.avoid: The colour code is explained only in the caption, with no in-figure legend, and repeating the full prefix on every line makes the figure dense.

core.what: decoding unrolled as nine left-aligned lines, one per iteration, each repeating the accepted prefix in black and ending in that iteration's coloured accepted, rejected and corrected tokens

relations.form: nine stacked rows of the same growing sentence, every row starting at [START] in the same column so each new iteration's tokens appear at the right end
the method acts on a real token sequence: each token underlined by a tick-ended bracket that marks its boundaries, with rejected draft tokens struck through in place
within a row, accepted draft tokens, a rejected token and the target model's correction follow left to right

channels.colour: black = prefix accepted in earlier iterations; green = draft-model tokens accepted this iteration; red with strike-through = the rejected draft token; blue = the token the target model supplies; one meaning each, keyed only in the caption
channels.shape: tick-ended brackets under each token = token boundaries
channels.line: strike-through = rejection
channels.frame: none

quality.strengths: The unrolled rows make 'several tokens per target call' visible as length: each line's coloured tail is the progress of one iteration; the data is a real sentence with real token boundaries; colour has one meaning per hue.
quality.weaknesses: Neither model is drawn, so which model proposes and which verifies is carried only by colour and the caption; most of the area repeats the black prefix while the new part (the coloured tail) is small; single-character rejected tokens such as ',' and '.' are hard to see; there is no in-figure key.

figures.lesson: Explain a decoding algorithm with a real sentence growing line by line, colouring each step's new tokens by outcome and striking through rejected ones.

figures.title: SplitFed: When Federated Learning Meets Split Learning

between each client and the Main Server, a green arrow carries the smashed data (last layer's activations) right and an orange arrow returns its gradients left

figures.title: Self-Supervised Learning of Physics-Guided Reconstruction Neural Networks without Fully-Sampled Reference Data

taxonomy.task: physics-guided unrolled MRI reconstruction

arrangement.units: lettered panels: blue-outlined pale-blue / pale-yellow boxes for iterations, grey-filled blue-outlined containers for the network detail

arrangement.shared: x^(0) feeds every DC block via one grey line

insights.flow: Left to right throughout; (a) closes a loop back to x^(i), (b) chains frames with an ellipsis, (c) has long skip lines under the slabs ending in blue circled + signs.
insights.avoid: Panel (c) shows a generic ResNet with no link line back to the R block it expands; draw a zoom connector from R to the ResNet container.

core.what: the unrolled network: one R-then-DC iteration drawn as a loop in panel (a), then repeated as a left-to-right chain of '1st' to 'T-th Iteration' boxes in panel (b)

relations.form: panel (a) draws one iteration as a cycle (R above, DC below, a return arrow); panel (b) unrolls it into two yellow iteration boxes joined by an ellipsis, with states x(0), z(0), x(1) ... x(T) labelled on the arrows
a grey line from the input x(0) runs over the top of panel (b) and drops into the DC block of every iteration
panel (c) opens the regulariser in a full-width bottom row: a grey 'ResNet' container of Conv and RB slabs with a long skip, and beside it a second grey container opening one 'Residual Block'
every panel reads left to right along a single horizontal axis

channels.colour: peach = the regulariser R and saturated green = data consistency DC, repeated identically in (a) and (b); in (c) light blue = Conv, green = RB, yellow = ReLU, red = xScale, so green means both DC and residual block
channels.shape: flat rectangles = blocks in (a) and (b); 3-D perspective slabs = layers in (c); a blue circle with + = addition
channels.line: black arrows = data flow; the grey line in (b) = the shared input to every DC; long underneath lines in (c) = skip connections
channels.frame: pale-blue box = one iteration in (a); pale-yellow box = one unrolled iteration in (b); grey containers with blue borders = network and block detail in (c)

quality.strengths: The same R and DC blocks keep their colour and shape from the loop in (a) to the unrolled chain in (b), so the reader sees that (b) is (a) repeated; states between iterations are labelled on the arrows; the long skip connections in (c) are short-path horizontals under the chain.
quality.weaknesses: Panel (c) is not tied to R by tint or a callout (R is peach, the ResNet container grey), so the zoom must be read from text; green means both DC and residual block; no data is drawn (no k-space, mask or image), so what DC enforces and what is input is invisible; the three panels give equal visual weight to the routine ResNet detail and the unrolling.

figures.lesson: Draw the iteration three ways in one figure - a single R/DC loop, the unrolled row of framed iterations, then the regulariser's layers as 3-D slabs - keeping R peach and DC green so both carry from the loop into the unrolled copies.

relations.form: each tier runs left to right; the bottom row turns up on the right into attention, the middle row's output loops back left and up to the post-net, and the top row runs right through the spectrogram to the vocoder
a line from the Bidirectional LSTM rises and runs left into a grey Location Sensitive Attention box, which exchanges a pair of up/down arrows with the 2 LSTM Layers box above it
the 2 LSTM Layers output forks into two stacked Linear Projection boxes, one going on to a 'Stop Token' output box, the other to the spectrogram path

the autoregressive feedback is one horizontal line from the upper Linear Projection running left above the decoder row to a junction that drops into the 2 Layer Pre-Net and rises into the Post-Net and the + node - drawn as a wire, not unrolled steps
the two-network split is shown by the mel spectrogram drawn as an actual heat-map plot between the feature-prediction network and the WaveNet vocoder

channels.colour: fill = component: blue encoder blocks, orange decoder blocks, grey attention, green vocoder, pale yellow = external inputs and outputs (Input Text, Stop Token, Waveform Samples) - one meaning
channels.shape: rounded rectangles = modules and I/O alike; a circled plus = residual addition; the intermediate is a plotted spectrogram image
channels.line: solid black arrows only; data flow, feedback and attention exchange all share one style

quality.strengths: the intermediate representation that splits the system in two is drawn as real data - a labelled mel-spectrogram plot sits between the predictor and WaveNet; encoder, decoder, attention and vocoder each have one fill, so the role of every block reads from colour
quality.weaknesses: the reading path zigzags (bottom row right, up, middle row right, back left along a long feedback wire, up, then right again); one horizontal line from the Linear Projection serves the autoregressive feedback to the Pre-Net, the Post-Net input and the residual + node, with a double-headed vertical arrow between Post-Net and Pre-Net that is hard to parse; the recurrence is a wire rather than unrolled steps, so the frame-by-frame generation is not visible

figures.lesson: Put the model's key intermediate representation in as a real rendered example (here a mel spectrogram with axes) at the hand-off point between two sub-networks, so the reader sees what flows between them.

figures.title: Editing Models with Task Arithmetic

taxonomy.task: editing pretrained models by adding, negating and combining task vectors
taxonomy.note: family other: model editing in weight space; architecture other: no network drawn, only weights as points and task vectors as arrows; depicts plots = 2-D vector diagrams

arrangement.units: four equal-width unframed panels separated by thin vertical rules, each titled with a letter and a name at the top-left
arrangement.inputs_as: weights as grey circles (θpre, θft) and task vectors as coloured arrows from an origin circle
arrangement.shared: the origin circle (pretrained weights) is redrawn at the base of the arrows in every panel

insights.structure: Four equal panels in one row: a definition panel followed by three operation panels, separated by thin vertical rules.
insights.data: Weights are grey circles and task vectors are arrows from an origin; each panel's equation is set beside the geometry that draws its terms.
insights.emphasis: In each operation panel the result vector is the one saturated arrow (orange in negation, purple in addition and analogy) among pale operand arrows.
insights.flow: Read panel by panel left to right; inside a panel arrows start at one origin circle and grey dashed lines complete the parallelogram or rectangle that constructs the result.
insights.avoid: An operand's colour changes between panels (τA is pale blue in (c) but pale yellow in (d); τB pink in (c), pale green in (d)) and the result is orange in (b) but purple elsewhere.

core.what: each edit drawn as vector geometry in weight space: arrows from one origin circle, a dashed parallelogram or rectangle constructing the sum, the result as the one saturated arrow

relations.form: task vectors are arrows between weight points (grey circles), and sums or differences are drawn as dashed parallelograms and rectangles from one origin
the three operations (negation, addition, analogy) sit in three equal panels side by side after the definition panel, each with its equation and an 'Example:' line in the same places
panel (a) defines τ = θft - θpre with an arrow from θpre to θft beside a dashed wiggly fine-tuning path, and the following panels reuse τ

channels.colour: pale arrows = operand task vectors, a saturated arrow = the vector being defined or produced (blue in (a), orange in (b), purple in (c) and (d)); operand hues are not kept across panels, so colour only separates operand from result within a panel
channels.shape: grey outlined circles = weights (points), straight arrows = task vectors
channels.line: solid arrows = vectors; grey dashed lines = construction lines (parallelogram sides, extension of τ) and in (a) the fine-tuning trajectory
channels.frame: no frames; thin vertical rules divide the panels

quality.strengths: each equation is drawn as its terms - operand arrows, a dashed parallelogram, the result arrow - so the method's arithmetic is visible as geometry; one panel per job (define, then three operations) with identical panel width and the same placement of equation and example; the result arrow is the most saturated mark in each panel
quality.weaknesses: operand colours change between panels (τA pale blue in (c), pale yellow in (d)) and the result is orange in (b) but purple in (c)-(d), so the colour code must be relearned per panel; the pale yellow τA in (d) nearly disappears against white; the 'Example' sentences under each panel use as much height as the diagrams

figures.lesson: Draw each arithmetic operation as geometry in one shared vector space - pale operand arrows, a dashed parallelogram, one saturated result arrow - with the equation above it as a caption, one panel per operation.

figures.title: TD-MPC2: Scalable, Robust World Models for Continuous Control

taxonomy.task: model-based continuous control with a decoder-free latent world model

arrangement.units: three unframed time-step columns side by side on whitespace, linked at latent level
arrangement.inputs_as: real rendered frames s_1..s_3 of the agent, one per column, with bold math labels at their lower left
arrangement.losses_at: not drawn; predicted a-hat, r-hat, q-hat sit as bold red symbols at the tips of three arrows above each latent
arrangement.shared: the encoder is redrawn identically under each column (same trapezoid and label)
